title: Conjugates
notes: Open with the envelope viewpoint. A closed convex function can be read from the affine functions sitting below it, and the conjugate is the ledger that records which intercept each slope needs. Keep the word price attached to slope p: p tells us how valuable one more unit of x is in the dual comparison.

title: Slope Price View
notes: Ask students to imagine choosing a price p before choosing x. The expression p x - f(x) is net profit after paying the cost f(x). The conjugate f*(p) is the best possible profit at that price, so changing p changes which primal point is worth producing.

title: Supremum Of Affine Gaps
notes: This slide converts the picture into the definition. For each fixed p, graph the vertical gaps between the affine reward p x and the cost f(x). The supremum of those gaps is f*(p). For a convex cost, the winning x is usually where the supporting line has slope p.

title: Support Lines
notes: Emphasize that the pair (p, f*(p)) is not abstract decoration: it writes the affine lower bound h_p(x)=p x - f*(p). When the line touches f, it certifies both Fenchel equality and a subgradient relation. When it does not touch, it still remains below f.

title: Quadratic Example
notes: Use the quadratic as the calibration example because every object is explicit. The maximizing x satisfies p=q x, and substituting that x gives f*(p)=p squared over two q. The key visual message is reciprocal curvature: steep primal bowls produce shallow dual bowls.

title: Indicator / Support Pair
notes: Now replace a numerical cost by a feasibility-only cost. The indicator of C charges zero inside C and infinity outside, so the conjugate searches only over feasible points. That search is exactly the support function of C, choosing whichever boundary point maximizes the current slope.

title: Norm / Dual Norm Pair
notes: For a norm, the conjugate is an indicator rather than another finite norm. If p stays inside the dual unit ball, p dot x never beats the norm by a positive unbounded amount. If p leaves that ball, scaling x in the exposing direction makes p dot x minus the norm diverge.

title: Biconjugate Picture
notes: The biconjugate keeps only information visible to affine lower certificates. Any nonconvex bump, missing boundary value, or upward discontinuity that cannot be certified from below disappears. What remains is the closed convex envelope recovered by taking all support lines back to the primal side.

title: Closed Convex Recovery
notes: State the recovery theorem in operational terms. For a closed proper convex f, conjugating twice returns f. For a general function, the same operation returns the closed convex minorant generated by the affine lower bounds. Closedness is doing real work here, not cosmetic work.

title: Fenchel Inequality
notes: Fenchel inequality is the one-line certificate that every later duality argument will reuse. Since f*(p) is the supremum of p x minus f(x), every particular x gives a lower candidate. Rearranging gives p x less than or equal to f(x)+f*(p).

title: Subgradient Equality Case
notes: Equality is the diagnostic condition. If p is a subgradient at x, the affine function with slope p supports f at x, so the Fenchel gap is zero. Conversely, zero gap means the supporting inequality is tight at x, which is exactly the subgradient certificate.

title: Numerical Conjugate Sampling
notes: Treat the grid computation as a sanity check, not as a theorem. Sampling a finite set of x-values approximates the supremum defining f*(p). The resulting table should show nonnegative Fenchel gaps and exact zeros when p matches the gradient in the quadratic model.

title: Failure Modes
notes: Close the technical body by naming the common traps. A conjugate can be infinite outside its natural domain, finite sampling can miss the true supremum, nonclosed functions may not return under biconjugacy, and reversing inequalities under conjugacy is easy to forget.

title: Recap
notes: End by asking for certificates. Given a proposed conjugate value, students should identify the primal x that attains or approximates the supremum, draw the supporting affine line, compute the Fenchel gap, and decide whether biconjugacy should recover the original function or its closed convex envelope.
